NEW YORK (CNN) -- Fans of Michael Jackson lined the streets outside Harlem's Apollo Theater on Tuesday for a chance to pay their respects to the late "King of Pop" at the hall that helped launch his career. A hat and glittery glove represent Michael Jackson at the Apollo Theater tribute. The crowd stood eight to 10 abreast in the sun and 80-degree weather for 10 blocks, waiting for hours for a chance to enter the theater. Fans were allowed in 600 at a time, where they lay flowers and other mementos at the foot of the stage and danced to Jackson's music as it played over the sound system. "We left our house at 4 o'clock in the morning and got here at 9, and we were lucky to get here," said Angela Staples, who came to New York from Pennsylvania with her daughter Jasmine. "I'm so happy about the outpouring of love and the crowd and the people. It's so respectful to Michael." Those in the hall observed a moment of silence at 5:26 p.m. -- the time Jackson was pronounced dead Thursday in Los Angeles, California. The cause of the 50-year-old singer's death has not yet been determined. An autopsy on the 50-year-old singer was was inconclusive, leaving authorities waiting on the results of toxicology tests to determine what killed him. Fans have been gathering outside the theater since last week to remember Jackson, who at age 9 won a 1967 Apollo amateur night showcase with his brothers in the group the Jackson 5. "While he went on from the Apollo stage to achieve international fame on an unprecedented level, to us and all of you, he's family because he started out here," said Jonelle Procope, the legendary venue's CEO. Jackson became an idol of both black and white fans and was among the first African-American artists to get widespread play on the music-video channel MTV. But in later years, he was known more for a roller-coaster personal life, including extensive plastic surgery, financial woes and a 1995 trial and acquittal on child-molestation charges. The Rev. Al Sharpton, the New York civil rights activist who became a friend of the Jackson family, urged Jackson's fans not to let critics "scandalize" a groundbreaking performer. "Michael wasn't no freak," Sharpton said. "Michael was a genius. Michael was an innovator. You can't take someone with extraordinary skills, extraordinary talent, and make him an ordinary person. He was extraordinary. He lived extraordinarily, and we love him with an extraordinary passion." The Apollo had been one of the top venues for jazz, gospel and soul artists for decades before the Jacksons' breakthrough.  Sharpton said the theater was home to "the best and the baddest." "You've got to come from the stage of the Apollo and go all over the world to understand Michael," Sharpton said. "We understand his journey, because we were with him every step of the way." The Jackson brothers' amateur night win led to a $1,000 deal for 31 shows at the Apollo, said Bobby Schiffman, whose family owned the theater. "Shortly after their appearance, Diana Ross took them on an NBC special that she did, and there was no looking back after that. They just skyrocketed," Schiffman said. Jackson at the time "was a sweet little boy," he said. "He was extremely talented, extremely easy to get along with," Schiffman said. "He always had a smile on his face, and it was a pleasure to see him working in the theater." CNN's Aspen Steib contributed to this report.

# Fans Gather at Apollo Theater to Honor Michael Jackson's Legacy

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Fans of Michael Jackson lined the streets outside Harlem's Apollo Theater on Tuesday, eager for the opportunity to pay their respects to the late "King of Pop" at the very venue that helped launch his career. Inside, a hat and a glittering glove stood as poignant symbols of Jackson at the theater's tribute.

Undeterred by the sweltering 80-degree heat, the crowd stretched eight to ten people deep across ten city blocks, patiently waiting hours for their turn to enter. Fans were admitted in groups of 600, where they laid flowers and other mementos at the foot of the stage, swaying and dancing to Jackson's music as it echoed through the sound system.

"We left our house at 4 o'clock in the morning and arrived at 9, and we still felt lucky to get here," said Angela Staples, who traveled from Pennsylvania with her daughter Jasmine to attend. "I'm so moved by this outpouring of love—the crowd, the people. It's such a respectful tribute to Michael."

At 5:26 p.m., attendees inside the hall observed a moment of silence, marking the exact time Jackson had been pronounced dead the previous Thursday in Los Angeles. The cause of the 50-year-old singer's death remains undetermined; an initial autopsy proved inconclusive, leaving authorities to await toxicology results for definitive answers.

Devoted fans had been gathering outside the theater since the previous week to honor Jackson, who at just nine years old triumphed at a 1967 Apollo amateur night alongside his brothers in the Jackson 5.

"While he went on from the Apollo stage to achieve international fame on an unprecedented scale, to us—and to all of you—he remains family, because this is where his journey began," said Jonelle Procope, CEO of the legendary venue.

Jackson captivated audiences across racial lines, becoming an idol to both Black and white fans alike, and stood among the first African-American artists to receive widespread exposure on MTV. Yet in his later years, public attention often shifted toward his turbulent personal life—marked by extensive plastic surgery, financial difficulties, and a highly publicized 1995 trial that ended in his acquittal on child molestation charges.

The Rev. Al Sharpton, the New York civil rights leader and longtime friend of the Jackson family, implored fans not to let critics tarnish the legacy of a trailblazing performer. "Michael wasn't some freak," Sharpton declared. "Michael was a genius. Michael was an innovator. You cannot take someone with such extraordinary skill and talent and reduce him to something ordinary. He was extraordinary. He lived an extraordinary life, and we love him with an extraordinary passion."

For decades before the Jackson family's breakthrough, the Apollo had reigned as one of the premier venues for jazz, gospel, and soul performers. Sharpton noted that the theater had long been home to "the best and the baddest."

"You have to come from the stage of the Apollo and travel the world to truly understand Michael," Sharpton said. "We understood his journey because we walked alongside him every step of the way."

The Jackson brothers' amateur night victory secured them a $1,000 contract for 31 performances at the Apollo, recalled Bobby Schiffman, whose family once owned the theater. "Shortly after their appearance, Diana Ross featured them on an NBC special she hosted, and from there, there was no looking back. They simply skyrocketed," Schiffman said.

At the time, Jackson "was a sweet little boy," he reminisced. "He was extremely talented, remarkably easy to work with. He always had a smile on his face, and it was truly a pleasure to watch him perform at the theater."

*CNN's Aspen Steib contributed to this report.*

# Fans Gather at Apollo Theater to Honor Michael Jackson

NEW YORK (CNN) -- On Tuesday, crowds of Michael Jackson admirers formed long lines outside Harlem's Apollo Theater, hoping to honor the "King of Pop" at the very venue that had once helped propel his career forward. Inside, a tribute featuring Jackson's signature hat and sequined glove marked his memory.

Spanning ten city blocks, the crowd packed together eight to ten people wide, enduring hours in the sweltering 80-degree heat for their turn to step inside. Theater staff admitted visitors in groups of 600, allowing them to place flowers and keepsakes near the stage while Jackson's songs filled the air through the sound system.

"We set out from home at 4 a.m. and arrived by 9, and even then we felt fortunate to make it," recalled Angela Staples, who traveled from Pennsylvania with her daughter Jasmine. "Seeing all this love pour out, the size of the crowd, everyone here—it means so much. This is such a fitting show of respect for Michael."

At exactly 5:26 p.m.—marking the moment Jackson's death was officially declared last Thursday in Los Angeles—those gathered inside fell silent in tribute. Medical examiners have yet to determine what caused the 50-year-old's death; while an autopsy was performed, it didn't yield conclusive answers, so officials are now awaiting toxicology results for more information.

Devoted followers had already been congregating near the theater for days prior, drawn by memories of Jackson's history there. Back in 1967, a 9-year-old Michael had triumphed at the Apollo's amateur night alongside his brothers as the Jackson 5.

Jonelle Procope, who heads the historic theater, reflected: "Even though his journey took him from this stage to global superstardom unlike anything seen before, he remains one of our own, part of our family—because this is where his story began."

Transcending racial boundaries, Jackson captured the devotion of fans across all backgrounds and broke barriers as one of the first Black artists to receive heavy rotation on MTV. However, his later years drew more attention for personal turmoil—numerous cosmetic surgeries, mounting debts, and a highly publicized 1995 trial where he was cleared of child molestation charges.

Civil rights figure Rev. Al Sharpton, a longtime friend of the Jackson family from New York, called on fans to resist letting detractors tarnish the legacy of such a pioneering artist. "Michael wasn't some kind of freak," he insisted. "He was a genius, a true innovator. Someone with that level of extraordinary gift and talent can't simply be reduced to ordinary. Everything about him was extraordinary—how he lived, how we loved him. Our passion for him matches his own remarkable nature."

Long before the Jackson brothers made their mark, the Apollo had already established itself as a premier stage for jazz, gospel, and soul performers across several decades. Sharpton described it as the birthplace of "the best and the baddest" talent.

"To truly understand Michael, you have to trace his path from that Apollo stage out into the entire world," Sharpton explained. "We know his journey intimately, because we walked alongside him through every part of it."

Bobby Schiffman, whose family once owned the historic venue, recounted how the brothers' amateur night victory secured them a contract worth $1,000 for a series of 31 performances at the theater. "Not long after they performed there, Diana Ross featured them on her NBC television special, and from that point forward, there was no stopping them—they shot straight to stardom," he said.

Schiffman remembered young Michael fondly: "He was such a sweet kid back then—incredibly gifted, and just easy to be around. He always wore a smile, and watching him perform at the theater was truly a joy."

*CNN's Aspen Steib contributed to this report.*

*By CNN Staff*

**NEW YORK (CNN)** — Thousands of grieving fans converged on Harlem's famed Apollo Theater Thursday night, transforming the historic marquee into an impromptu shrine as news spread of Michael Jackson's sudden death at age 50.

By nightfall, the sidewalk outside the theater on West 125th Street was awash in candles, flowers, and handwritten tributes. Fans young and old sang "Man in the Mirror" and "Billie Jean" through tears, while others simply stood in stunned silence, staring up at the marquee that read: "Michael Jackson 1958-2009. The Apollo Remembers a Legend."

"This is where it all started for him," said Loretta Simmons, 58, who says she saw the Jackson 5 perform at the Apollo as a teenager. "I had to come here tonight. There was nowhere else I could be."

The Apollo holds special significance in Jackson's story. It was here, in 1967, that a young Michael Jackson and his brothers won the theater's famous Amateur Night contest, a launching pad that many credit with helping propel the group — and Michael specifically — toward superstardom.

Theater officials confirmed they would hold a moment of silence Friday and were considering a larger tribute event in the coming days, given the outpouring of grief.

"The Apollo is where legends are born, and Michael Jackson was one of the greatest legends this stage has ever seen," said Apollo Theater spokesperson Kimberly Ellis. "It felt only right that his fans would gather here tonight."

The crowd, which authorities estimated grew to more than 3,000 people by 10 p.m., spilled into the street, blocking traffic as police moved in to manage the swelling numbers. Impromptu dance circles broke out as fans performed Jackson's signature moves, including the moonwalk, to blaring music from portable speakers.

Vendors quickly appeared selling t-shirts, buttons, and posters bearing Jackson's image, while others sold roses to mourners looking to add to the growing memorial at the theater's entrance.

"I didn't know him personally, but it feels like I lost a member of my family," said 34-year-old Darnell Whitfield, who traveled from Brooklyn as soon as he heard the news. "He gave us so much joy. The least we could do is come together and celebrate his life."

Jackson, who rose to fame as a child star with the Jackson 5 before becoming one of the best-selling solo artists in music history, died Thursday afternoon after suffering cardiac arrest at his rented Los Angeles home. He was pronounced dead at UCLA Medical Center. He had been preparing for a series of highly anticipated comeback concerts in London, scheduled to begin in July.

Similar scenes of mourning played out across the globe Thursday night, from outside Jackson's Neverland Ranch in California to Times Square, where his music videos played on jumbotrons to crowds of onlookers.

But for many at the Apollo, the connection felt personal and rooted in history.

"This theater made him, in a way," said longtime Harlem resident James Coley, 71. "And tonight, it's helping us say goodbye."

As the night wore on, organizers announced plans for a candlelight vigil to be held outside the theater through the weekend, with hopes that Harlem — and the Apollo — would serve as one of the central gathering points for fans mourning the King of Pop.

"He belonged to the world," said theater historian Curtis Reeves, "but tonight, in a very real sense, he belonged to Harlem."
